--- title: "Scheduling minimum gapped ESM events uniformly on a circle" subtitle: "A bounded question in point-process theory, arising from an experience-sampling design" draft: true # source document, not published; see index.qmd for the blog note author: "Tim Seidel" date: today format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 2 number-sections: true embed-resources: true code-tools: true fig-width: 8 fig-height: 4 df-print: kable execute: warning: false message: false knitr: opts_chunk: comment: "#>" collapse: true --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## What this document is A self-contained statement of a problem that arose in designing a psychological study, and that turns out to be a known model in statistical physics. I am an applied psychologist. I can state the problem, run simulations, and check a result numerically once I have it. I cannot derive it or check the statistical physics sources with 100% confidence. ::: # The applied problem {#sec-problem} Participants in said study carry a phone for 18 days. On each day they are sent $n = 6$ *pings*: a notification inviting them to fill in a short questionnaire about what they are doing and feeling at that moment. The design constraints are these. 1. **Every ping must be structurally identical.** The same notification, the same reminder chain, the same questionnaire, the same expiry rules. Nothing about a ping may depend on which ping of the day it is, because the pings are the replicated unit of measurement and any structural difference between them becomes a confound. 2. **A ping consists of an invitation plus an allowed window $t$** during which the participant may still open and complete the questionnaire. After $t$ the invitation expires and the ping is recorded as missed. 3. **Therefore every ping occupies an interval of fixed length $t$** on the time axis, beginning at the moment it is issued. 4. **No ping may be issued before the previous ping's interval has elapsed.** Two overlapping pings would mean two open questionnaires at once: the participant could answer them out of order, or answer one about the other's moment, and the platform cannot in general tell which. This is a hard constraint, not a preference. 5. **The pings must uniformly sample the participant's day.** The scientific claim the study makes is that the sampled moments are a representative sample of waking life. If some times of day are more likely to be sampled than others, the resulting picture of the person is distorted, and — because every participant is sampled by the same schedule — the distortion does not average out across the sample. Constraints 1–4 say the events cannot be too close together. Constraint 5 says the marginal distribution of event times must be flat. The tension between those two requirements is the entire problem. # Formalisation {#sec-formal} Fix a waking window of width $W$ minutes, from `start_h` to `end_h`. A schedule for one day is a vector of offsets $$ 0 \le t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_n < W, $$ measured in minutes after `start_h`. Constraints 1–4 impose a **hard core**: a minimum admissible separation $G \ge t$ between consecutive events. Constraint 5 asks for **constant first-order intensity**: the marginal density of event times, pooled over $k$ and over participants, should be uniform on $[0, W)$. So the object wanted is a point process on a bounded window with - a **fixed** number of points $n$ (not a random count — the design specifies six pings a day, and constraint 1 forbids treating them differently), - a hard-core exclusion at distance $G$, - constant first-order intensity across the window. Writing $S = W - nG$ for the *slack*, the design under study is ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} circ_config <- function(days = 18, slots = 6, start_h = 9, end_h = 21, min_gap = 90, window = 30) { cfg <- list(days = days, slots = slots, start_h = start_h, end_h = end_h, min_gap = min_gap, window = window) cfg$width <- (end_h - start_h) * 60 # W cfg$n <- days * slots cfg$slack <- cfg$width - slots * min_gap # S, the circular slack cfg$max_gap <- cfg$width - (slots - 1) * min_gap cfg } cfg <- circ_config() data.frame(symbol = c("W", "n", "G", "S", "t"), meaning = c("width of waking window (min)", "events per day", "minimum separation (min)", "slack, W - nG", "allowed response window (min)"), value = c(cfg$width, cfg$slots, cfg$min_gap, cfg$slack, cfg$window)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|symbol |meaning | value| |:------|:-----------------------------|-----:| |W |width of waking window (min) | 720| |n |events per day | 6| |G |minimum separation (min) | 90| |S |slack, W - nG | 180| |t |allowed response window (min) | 30|
::: ::: $G = 90$ against $t = 30$ is not slack for its own sake: the full ping chain (notification, reminder email, invitation, expiry, grace) occupies up to 45 (which is variable between ESM Studies) minutes in the worst case, and 90 is that floor with margin. # The construction in use {#sec-construction} The day is treated not as an interval $[0, W)$ but as a **circle** of circumference $W$, identifying $0 \equiv W$. Five steps: 1. Draw $U_1, \dots, U_{n-1}$ iid uniform on $(0,1)$, sort them, and take the $n$ spacings $D_j$. These are $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$, i.e. uniform on the standard simplex. 2. Set $s_j = G + S D_j$. Then $s_j \ge G$ and $\sum_j s_j = W$: the $n$ gaps close the circle exactly, and $s$ is uniform over the admissible gap set. 3. Partial-sum the gaps into positions $c_k$ on the circle. 4. Draw a phase $\Phi \sim \mathrm{U}[0, W)$ independently and rotate: $t^*_k = (\Phi + c_k) \bmod W$. 5. Sort and floor to whole minutes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} circ_offsets <- function(cfg) { n <- cfg$slots e <- diff(c(0, sort(runif(n - 1)), 1)) * cfg$slack # steps 1-2 s <- cfg$min_gap + e phase <- runif(1) * cfg$width # step 4 sort(floor((phase + cumsum(c(0, s[-n]))) %% cfg$width)) } ``` ::: The natural comparison places the points on an **interval with walls** instead: draw $n$ uniforms on the reduced interval $[0, W - (n-1)G)$, sort, and re-inflate by the reserved gaps. This is uniform over admissible *position vectors on a line*. I am quite convinces that this is not a straw man. Interval-based schedulers — the walled geometry, usually with the minimum gap imposed by rejecting and redrawing rather than built into the construction — are what experience-sampling platforms deploy today, and I have read the scheduling code of one widely used open-source platform to confirm it and a few example ESM papers that suggest it. The comparison below is therefore between the construction I use and the construction the field is currently running (if they are not running fixed times with jitter or something else, which is obviously not superior with regards to uniform distribution. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} seq_offsets <- function(cfg) { slack <- cfg$width - (cfg$slots - 1) * cfg$min_gap # line, not circle sort(runif(cfg$slots) * slack) + (seq_len(cfg$slots) - 1) * cfg$min_gap } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} draw_days <- function(cfg, n_days = 20000, sampler = circ_offsets) { offs <- vapply(seq_len(n_days), function(i) sampler(cfg), numeric(cfg$slots)) data.frame(slot = rep(seq_len(cfg$slots), times = n_days), off = as.vector(offs)) } d_circ <- draw_days(cfg, 20000, circ_offsets) d_seq <- draw_days(cfg, 20000, seq_offsets) ``` ::: # What is already established {#sec-known} The construction is not new, and the relevant results are known. The initial search suggests that physics basically solved this and ESM scheduling has simply not picked up this method. Mapping the notation: my $W$ is a ring of circumference $L\sigma$, my $n$ is $N$ rods, my $G$ is the rod length $\sigma$ (hard-core diameter $d$), and my slack $S = W - nG$ is the free length. | result | status | source | |---|---|---| | gaps are $G + S \cdot \mathrm{Beta}(1, n-1)$ | classical | Pyke (1965), uniform spacings | | configuration volume on a ring is $L(L-N)^{N-1}$ | exact | Robledo & Rowlinson (1986), eq. (6.1) | | one-body density on a ring is constant in $x$ | exact | Robledo & Rowlinson (1986), eq. (6.6) | | two-body and higher are **not** constant | exact | Robledo & Rowlinson (1986), §6 | | on a line with walls, wall effects reach $(N-1)d$ from each end | exact | Leff & Coopersmith (1967) | | flat central region on a line iff $L \ge 2(N-1)d$ | exact | Leff & Coopersmith (1967) | | periodic BC preserves homogeneity, fixed BC does not | — | Kratky (1980), Table I | | random start on a circular arrangement equalises inclusion probabilities | exact | Lahiri (1952), circular systematic sampling | Two of these, I think, show the properties of the sampler almost exactly: **Robledo & Rowlinson eq. (6.1)**, $V^r_{L,N} = L(L-N)^{N-1}$, factorises exactly as the construction above: the prefactor $L$ is the rotational freedom (my phase $\Phi$), and $(L-N)^{N-1}$ is the simplex of free gaps with free length $L-N$ (my $S$). The sampler in @sec-construction is a uniform sampler on the configuration space whose volume this is. **Their §6 also states the first-order/second-order split** that the rest of my work rests on: a system with repeating boundary conditions is uniform in the one-body sense, while the two-body and higher distribution functions are not. # Numerical evidence {#sec-numerics} ## The circle is flat; the interval is not ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all2 <- rbind(transform(d_circ, sampler = "circular"), transform(d_seq, sampler = "sequential")) ggplot(all2, aes(off, fill = sampler)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, boundary = 0, colour = NA) + geom_hline(yintercept = nrow(d_circ) / (cfg$width / 10), colour = COL["theory"], linewidth = 0.6) + facet_wrap(~sampler) + scale_fill_manual(values = COL, guide = "none") + labs(x = "minutes after start_h", y = "events per 10-min bin") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Pooled time-of-day density, 20 000 days each. Red line is the uniform expectation.](collaboration_brief_files/figure-html/fig-flatness-1.png){#fig-flatness width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} flatness <- function(off, cfg, bin = 10) { cnt <- as.numeric(table(cut(off, seq(0, cfg$width, by = bin), right = FALSE))) data.frame(cv = sd(cnt) / mean(cnt), cv_noise = 1 / sqrt(mean(cnt))) } do.call(rbind, lapply(split(all2, all2$sampler), function(g) cbind(sampler = g$sampler[1], flatness(g$off, cfg)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| |sampler | cv| cv_noise| |:----------|:----------|---------:|---------:| |circular |circular | 0.0234107| 0.0244949| |sequential |sequential | 0.3749330| 0.0244949|
::: ::: The circular sampler sits at the counting-noise floor. The interval sampler exceeds it by an order of magnitude, with mass piled at both ends. ## The interval sampler matches Leff & Coopersmith exactly {#sec-lc} Their eq. (15) gives the one-body density for $N$ hard cores of diameter $d$ in a box $[0, L]$. With $M = N-1$ and $\Delta = L - Md$: $$ D_1(x) \;\propto\; \sum_{k=0}^{M} \binom{M}{k}\,(x - kd)^{k}\, \bigl[\Delta - (x - kd)\bigr]^{M-k}\, \Theta_k(x), \qquad \Theta_k(x) = \mathbb{1}\{kd \le x \le \Delta + kd\}. $$ Implemented up to normalisation, then normalised to integrate to $n$: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lc_D1 <- function(x, N, d, L) { M <- N - 1; Delta <- L - M * d stopifnot(Delta > 0) sapply(x, function(xx) { k <- 0:M; y <- xx - k * d keep <- (y >= 0) & (y <= Delta) if (!any(keep)) return(0) sum(choose(M, k[keep]) * y[keep]^k[keep] * (Delta - y[keep])^(M - k[keep])) }) } lc_density <- function(cfg, G = cfg$min_gap, grid_n = 1441) { g <- seq(0, cfg$width, length.out = grid_n) v <- lc_D1(g, cfg$slots, G, cfg$width) data.frame(x = g, dens = v / (sum(v) * (g[2] - g[1])) * cfg$slots) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_lc <- 200000 d_lc <- draw_days(cfg, n_lc, seq_offsets) lc <- lc_density(cfg) ggplot(d_lc, aes(off)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density) * cfg$slots), binwidth = 10, boundary = 0, fill = COL["sequential"], colour = NA) + geom_line(data = lc, aes(x, dens), colour = COL["theory"], linewidth = 0.7) + labs(x = "minutes after start_h", y = "intensity (events per minute)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Simulated sequential sampler (bars) against Leff & Coopersmith eq. (15) (line), at G = 90, 200 000 days.](collaboration_brief_files/figure-html/fig-lc-1.png){#fig-lc width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} br <- seq(0, cfg$width, by = 10) emp <- as.numeric(table(cut(d_lc$off, br, right = FALSE))) / (n_lc * 10) pred <- approx(lc$x, lc$dens, head(br, -1) + 5)$y c(max_rel_dev = round(max(abs(emp - pred)) / mean(emp), 4), rms_rel_dev = round(sqrt(mean((emp - pred)^2)) / mean(emp), 4), correlation = round(cor(emp, pred), 6)) #> max_rel_dev rms_rel_dev correlation #> 0.016200 0.007100 0.999829 ``` ::: The worst 10-minute bin sits within a few per cent of the analytic curve and the root-mean-square deviation is well below that, both shrinking as $N^{-1/2}$ with the number of simulated days. The mapping between my sampler and their model is therefore confirmed numerically, not merely asserted. ## The design has no flat region at all Their criterion: a central region in which $D_1$ is constant exists **iff** $L \ge 2(N-1)d$, and it is $[(N-1)d,\; L-(N-1)d]$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} crit <- function(n, G, W) { reach <- (n - 1) * G data.frame(n, G, W, reach_from_each_end = reach, need_W = 2 * reach, central_region = if (W >= 2 * reach) sprintf("[%g, %g]", reach, W - reach) else "EMPTY") } rbind(crit(6, 90, 720), crit(6, 72, 720), crit(6, 60, 720), crit(5, 90, 720), crit(6, 90, 900)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| n| G| W| reach_from_each_end| need_W|central_region | |--:|--:|---:|-------------------:|------:|:--------------| | 6| 90| 720| 450| 900|EMPTY | | 6| 72| 720| 360| 720|[360, 360] | | 6| 60| 720| 300| 600|[300, 420] | | 5| 90| 720| 360| 720|[360, 360] | | 6| 90| 900| 450| 900|[450, 450] |
::: ::: At the operating point the required window is 900 minutes and the actual window is 720. **The interval sampler is non-uniform across the whole day — there is no interior region where it is flat.** Restoring one would require a 15-hour waking window, or at most 5 pings, or a minimum separation of 72 minutes; all three are excluded by constraints 1–4. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(60, 72, 90), function(G) { z <- lc_density(cfg, G); z$G <- sprintf("G = %d", G); z })) bands <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(60, 72, 90), function(G) { r <- (cfg$slots - 1) * G if (cfg$width >= 2 * r) data.frame(G = sprintf("G = %d", G), lo = r, hi = cfg$width - r) else NULL })) ggplot(grid, aes(x, dens)) + { if (!is.null(bands)) geom_rect(data = bands, inherit.aes = FALSE, aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf), fill = COL["ok"], alpha = 0.15) } + geom_line(colour = COL["theory"], linewidth = 0.6) + facet_wrap(~G) + labs(x = "minutes after start_h", y = "intensity") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Leff & Coopersmith D1(x) at three minimum separations. Green marks the flat central region where one exists.](collaboration_brief_files/figure-html/fig-lc-crit-1.png){#fig-lc-crit width=768} ::: ::: For comparison, the circular sampler is flat at every one of these settings, by construction — this is Robledo & Rowlinson eq. (6.6). # The open question {#sec-open} The literature gives me: - the **ring** at *fluctuating* $N$ — Robledo & Rowlinson, grand canonical; - the **line with walls** at *fixed* $N$ — Leff & Coopersmith, canonical. What I think ESM actually runs is **fixed $n$ on a ring**, and that combination is in neither. It matters because constraint 1 fixes $n$ exactly: the study delivers six pings a day, not a Poisson number averaging six. Concretely, what I would like is the **pair correlation function $g(r)$ for $n$ hard cores of diameter $G$ placed uniformly on a circle of circumference $W$, at fixed $n$** — and, if it comes cheaply, the corresponding Bartlett spectrum. My guess, worth exactly what it cost, is that the Leff & Coopersmith §II factorisation carries around the wrap with the $n+1$ interval factors becoming $n$ cyclic ones, and that the answer is a ratio of simplex volumes with inclusion–exclusion over how many cores fit in the arc. I have not been able to carry that through. What I have instead is a simulation. It shows structure at multiples of $W/n$ that does not vanish with sample size, and a Bartlett spectrum reaching $S(n) \approx 1.75$ against a binomial reference of 1. I currently report those as empirical facts and decline to interpret them, which is unsatisfying — and it leaves the one question a reviewer will ask (what does the residual second-order structure cost when estimating a dynamic model on this data?) unanswerable. There is also a result from the signal-processing side that I think bears on this and would like a second opinion on: Srivastava & Sengupta (2011) prove that under a minimum-separation constraint, no point-process sampling scheme is alias-free for the class of all spectra, though it can be for band-limited ones. If I read that correctly, the residual structure at $W/n$ is not a defect of my construction but the unavoidable price of constraint 4, which would be worth saying plainly. # The ask {#sec-ask} Three things, in decreasing order of how much they would help: 1. **The fixed-$n$ ring pair correlation function** (@sec-open), or a pointer to where it is already written down. I can verify any candidate expression numerically within a day. 2. **A check on whether the mapping in @sec-known is stated correctly**, particularly whether calling this the canonical hard-rod-on-a-ring model is right or whether there is a better-established name for it. 3. **A judgement on whether the Srivastava & Sengupta reading in @sec-open is sound.** What is on offer in return: co-authorship on a methods paper aimed at *Behavior Research Methods* or *Psychological Methods*. The applied side — why experience-sampling designs need this, what the current practice gets wrong, and what it costs — is written and simulated. A full companion notebook derives and numerically verifies the properties of the sampler in about two thousand lines, including the design consequences and an equivalence check against the shipped production code. This document is the mathematical core of it, extracted. # References {#sec-references} - Kratky, K. W. (1980). New boundary conditions for computer experiments of thermodynamic systems. *Journal of Computational Physics*, 37, 205–217. — Table I: fixed boundary conditions fail homogeneity, periodic ones do not. - Lahiri, D. B. (1952). A method for sample selection providing unbiased ratio estimates. *Bulletin of the ISI*, 33(2), 133–140. — Circular systematic sampling; a random start on a circular arrangement. - Leff, H. S., & Coopersmith, M. H. (1967). Translational invariance properties of a finite one-dimensional hard-core fluid. *Journal of Mathematical Physics*, 8, 306–314. — Canonical, fixed $N$, hard walls; the $(N-1)d$ reach and the $L \ge 2(N-1)d$ criterion used in @sec-lc. - Pyke, R. (1965). Spacings. *JRSS-B*, 27(3), 395–449. — Uniform spacings; Dirichlet and Beta results behind steps 1–2. - Robledo, A., & Rowlinson, J. S. (1986). The distribution of hard rods on a line of finite length. *Molecular Physics*, 58(4), 711–721. — §6, repeating boundary conditions: eq. (6.1) the ring configuration volume, eq. (6.6) constant one-body density, eqs. (6.7)–(6.8) the grand-canonical ring pair distribution. - Salsburg, Z. W., Zwanzig, R. W., & Kirkwood, J. G. (1953). Molecular distribution functions in a one-dimensional fluid. *Journal of Chemical Physics*, 21, 1098. - Schreiner, W., & Kratky, K. W. (1983). Finiteness effects in computer simulation of fluids with spherical boundary conditions. *Molecular Physics*, 50(3), 435–452. - Srivastava, R., & Sengupta, D. (2011). Effect of inter-sample spacing constraint on spectrum estimation with irregular sampling. *IEEE Transactions on Information Theory*, 57(7). — No point-process sampling scheme is alias-free for all spectra under a minimum-separation constraint. - Tonks, L. (1936). The complete equation of state of one, two and three-dimensional gases of hard elastic spheres. *Physical Review*, 50, 955.
